Question: Two tour guides are leading six tourists. The guides decide to split up. Each tourist must choose one of the guides, but with the stipulation that each guide must take at least one tourist. How many different groupings of guides and tourists are possible?
Solution:
First allow either guide to receive no tourists. Each of the six tourists has two choices, so the multiplication principle gives
\[
2^6=64
\]
assignments. Each assignment determines exactly one grouping, and every grouping determines each tourist's choice, so nothing is omitted or counted twice.

A guide has no tourists precisely when all six choose the other guide. There are exactly two such assignments, one for each choice of the guide who receives everyone. Removing these two distinct exceptions leaves
\[
64-2=\boxed{62}.
\]
The answer is \(\text{D}\).
